messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mele is a 19-year-old Pacific Islander woman who works on a commercial fishing boat and has been in a relationship for the past year. She came to treatment months after witnessing a violent accident at the docks. At the end of a long day unloading catch, one of the deckhands wheeled a bicycle through the crowded loading area. A truck reversed unexpectedly, there was shouting, the scrape and crash of metal, and then the sickening sight of the cyclist struck and thrown to the ground while people froze for a split second before running toward him. Mele remembers hearing footsteps pounding behind her as others rushed past, and the confused mix of shouted instructions, brakes, and impact sounds. She had moved toward him too, but not fast enough in her own mind. What stayed with her was the conviction that she should have done more, should have protected him somehow, and failed.

In the weeks after, the reminders were woven through her daily life on the docks and around town. A bicycle leaning against a fence near the harbor, footsteps coming up behind her on the pier before dawn, or the clatter of related sounds around loading equipment could hit her with a surge that arrived in her body before she had time to think. Sometimes the memory came with no clear picture at all, only the full emotional force of that moment—dread, horror, guilt—breaking through while she was baiting lines or sorting fish. At other times the memory forced its way in uninvited and she would hear the crash again. Those moments did not feel like ordinary remembering. They seemed to prove to her that her body had become an enemy, reacting as if she were still there, still failing.

That meaning hardened quickly. Mele had come to believe that if she could not even control her own body’s reactions, she might not be able to control her anger either. She was frightened by how sharply she snapped when startled, especially by footsteps behind her, and she worried that one day she would lash out and do something terrible. The guilt of having failed to protect someone fed that fear; when the memory came back, it was never just sadness but an accusation. Because she was already expecting danger, even ordinary delays began to feel ominous. If a boat was late returning or her boyfriend did not answer right away, her mind jumped to catastrophe. In that keyed-up state she noticed bicycles, sounds, and people approaching from behind almost before anything else, as if the world had narrowed around what might set her off.

She tried to manage this by keeping herself constantly occupied. On the boat she volunteered for extra tasks, stayed late cleaning gear, and took on more work than anyone asked of her because exhaustion felt safer than being alone with her thoughts. When she finally got home, she scrolled on her phone for hours or disappeared into videos and games until she could barely keep her eyes open. She also began avoiding sex with her partner; closeness made her feel trapped inside her own body, too aware of how quickly it could surge into alarm. These strategies made sense to her as ways to prevent the memory from breaking through, but they only tightened things. The more she overworked and distracted herself, the less room she had to process what she had witnessed, and when the memory did break in it felt even more abrupt and uncontrollable. After nights lost to screens and too little sleep, her concentration on the water worsened, and her body seemed even quicker to react before her mind caught up.

That left her increasingly convinced that something in her was dangerous and wrong. Each new jolt of fear when she heard footsteps behind her, each stab of panic at the sight of a bicycle near the docks, seemed to confirm both that she had failed that day and that she still could not get a grip on herself. She became more watchful of sounds around her, more likely to interpret delays as signs that something terrible had happened, and more reliant on work and her phone to blunt what followed. Her boyfriend noticed that she was distant and always half-elsewhere; crewmates noticed she missed instructions and stared off when metal clanged unexpectedly. What finally brought Mele in was a recent morning at work when a bicycle courier crossed the dock behind her and, at the same moment, running footsteps sounded on the planks. Her whole body recoiled before she knew why, and for a few seconds she was flooded with guilt and terror without any clear image. She was shaken less by the reminder itself than by what she made of it: that she might never be safe in her own body, might hurt someone if startled at the wrong moment, and might keep living as though danger was always just behind her. She is seeking help because she wants to stop feeling ruled by that fear, and because part of her still hopes she can be close to people again without the event crashing back in.
